newsitem.title: USA: BPA says using power sales to cut hydro spill rate.
newsitem.headline: BPA says using power sales to cut hydro spill rate.

text.p: The Bonneville Power Administration's (BPA) strategy for reducing hydropower dam spill this spring centers on aggressive marketing of expected surplus electricity, a BPA official said on Thursday.
Spill-reduction is critical to the survival of endangered fish species since high levels of dissolved gas caused by rushing water can be lethal for the fish.
Flows on the Snake River could be the highest in 68 years of record-keeping, while the Columbia River's flows are expected to be in the top 10 percent, a BPA spokesman said.

In a conference call with reporters, Robyn MacKay, BPA team leader for short term operations planning, said the main difference between the agency's response to expected high stream flows last year and this year is "real aggressive marketing and displacement deals."

But BPA said last week that those offers have met limited success due to a variety of factors including market expectations of lower spot prices this spring and constraints on interstate transmission lines.
"We do expect prices to continue to fall and we will be offering (daily displacement) energy," MacKay said.
She noted "the folks who hold out will only be able to get the light load power."
BPA anticipates a big surplus of off-peak power due to the need to run water through turbines around-the-clock.
So far, BPA has displaced with hydropower thermal generation from the Hermiston 440 megawatt (MW) plant, the Beaver 500 MW plant and the Gacsby 235 MW plant.
Another 475 MW of partial displacement sales in the Northwest have been concluded, the agency said.
MacKay confirmed that Mid-Columbia dam flows have been curbed this month at the request of states and tribes concerned that cool, dry weather in April could create problems for migrating fish.
The Grand Coulee project in Washington now stands at 1,240 feet, while its late-April flood control target will likely be 1,208 to 1,220 feet, she added.
